claim: Drosophila imaginal discs lose the ability to regenerate as they mature.
source: Like tissues of many organisms, Drosophila imaginal discs lose the ability to regenerate as they mature.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing reduced regeneration in late L3 compared to early L3 discs.

claim: The loss of regenerative capacity in imaginal discs coincides with reduced damage-responsive expression of multiple genes needed for regeneration.
source: This loss of regenerative capacity coincides with reduced damage-responsive expression of multiple genes needed for regeneration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data showing reduced expression of wg, Wnt6, Mmp1, and other genes in mature discs following damage.

claim: wg and Wnt6 are regulated by a single damage-responsive enhancer that becomes progressively inactivated via Polycomb-mediated silencing as discs mature.
source: We previously showed that two such genes, wg and Wnt6, are regulated by a single damage-responsive enhancer that becomes progressively inactivated via Polycomb-mediated silencing as discs mature (Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Harris et al., 2016) and is referenced as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Additional damage-responsive, maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancers exist near genes required for regeneration such as Mmp1.
source: Here we explore the generality of this mechanism and identify additional damage-responsive, maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancers, some near genes known to be required for regeneration such as Mmp1, and others near genes that we now show function in regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing DRMS enhancer activity at the Mmp1 locus.

claim: apontic (apt) curtails regeneration.
source: Using a novel GAL4-independent ablation system we characterize two DRMS-associated genes, apontic (apt), which curtails regeneration and CG9752/asperous (aspr), which promotes it.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that knockdown of apt improves regeneration.

claim: CG9752/asperous (aspr) promotes regeneration.
source: Using a novel GAL4-independent ablation system we characterize two DRMS-associated genes, apontic (apt), which curtails regeneration and CG9752/asperous (aspr), which promotes it.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that knockdown of aspr reduces regeneration.

claim: Reducing activity of the chromatin regulator extra sex combs (esc) can partially overcome the suppression of regeneration by silencing damage-responsive enhancers.
source: This mechanism of suppressing regeneration by silencing damage-responsive enhancers at multiple loci can be partially overcome by reducing activity of the chromatin regulator extra sex combs (esc).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing improved regeneration with esc knockdown.

claim: The hind limbs of Xenopus laevis progressively lose the ability to recover from amputation as the tadpole develops through juvenile stages.
source: The hind limbs of the anuran amphibian Xenopus laevis progressively lose the ability to recover from amputation as the tadpole develops through juvenile stages (Dent, 1962; Overton, 1963; Muneoka et al., 1986; Wolfe et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Damaged cardiac tissue can completely regenerate in newborn mice, while the same injury inflicted just 7 days later results in fibrosis and scarring.
source: Damaged cardiac tissue can completely regenerate in newborn mice, while the same injury inflicted just 7 days later results in fibrosis and scarring (Porrello et al., 2011; Porrello et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Loss of regenerative capacity with increasing maturity is observed in diverse tissues of mammals including humans.
source: This striking loss of regenerative capacity with increasing maturity is observed in diverse tissues of mammals (Reginelli et al., 1995; Porrello et al., 2011; Cox et al., 2014) including humans (Illingworth, 1974; King, 1979), and also in amphibians (Dent, 1962; Freeman, 1963; Beck et al., 2003; Slack et al., 2004) and invertebrates (Smith-Bolton et al., 2009; Halme et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research across different organisms.

claim: Many tissues continue their program of developmental growth even after they lose the ability to regenerate.
source: Remarkably, many of these same tissues continue their program of developmental growth even after they lose the ability to regenerate.
evidence: This is stated as an observation based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Imaginal discs readily regenerate at the beginning of the third larval instar (L3), but lose this ability over the course of L3.
source: Using these and other approaches, it was shown that imaginal discs readily regenerate at the beginning of the third larval instar (L3), but lose this ability over the course of L3 (Smith-Bolton et al., 2009; Halme et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Multiple genes known to be upregulated in response to damage show less robust expression in more mature discs, which correlates with the loss of regenerative capacity.
source: Multiple genes known to be upregulated in response to damage show less robust expression in more mature discs, which correlates with the loss of regenerative capacity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and is supported by data in the manuscript showing reduced expression of damage-responsive genes in late L3 discs.

claim: Genome-wide changes in chromatin accessibility are associated with regeneration following genetically-induced cell death in wing discs.
source: Recently it was shown that genome-wide changes in chromatin accessibility are associated with regeneration following genetically-induced cell death in wing discs (Vizcaya-Molina et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Wnt proteins play an important role in orchestrating regeneration in many organisms.
source: Wnt proteins play an important role in orchestrating regeneration in many organisms (Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Following damage, wg expression requires a damage-responsive enhancer, BRV118, located between wg and Wnt6.
source: Following damage, wg expression requires a damage-responsive enhancer, BRV118, located between wg and Wnt6 (Schubiger et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The BRV118 enhancer contains a damage-responsive module (BRV-B) containing multiple binding sites for the JNK-responsive transcription factor AP-1 that are essential for its damage-responsive activity.
source: We showed that this enhancer contains a damage-responsive module (BRV-B) containing multiple binding sites for the JNK-responsive transcription factor AP-1 and that these sites are essential for its damage-responsive activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: BRV-C can silence the damage-responsive expression mediated by BRV-B in cis in a maturity-dependent manner by promoting Polycomb-mediated silencing of the enhancer.
source: An adjacent and separate element, BRV-C, has no enhancer activity on its own, but can silence the damage-responsive expression mediated by BRV-B in cis in a maturity-dependent manner by promoting Polycomb-mediated silencing of the enhancer, characterized by highly localized H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: Restoring wg expression in late L3 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated excision of the silencing element BRV-C or by expression of wg did not restore regeneration.
source: Importantly, restoring wg expression in late L3 either by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated excision of the silencing element, BRV-C, or by expression of wg did not restore regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: The BRV-B module contains multiple AP-1 binding sites that are conserved in other Drosophila species.
source: The damage-responsive module of BRV118, BRV-B, contains multiple AP-1 binding sites that are essential for its ability to respond to tissue damage, and which are also found in the corresponding enhancer regions of other Drosophila species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing conservation across species.

claim: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins are necessary for the silencing activity of BRV-C.
source: We have previously shown that multiple elements in the module required for silencing the enhancer in mature discs (BRV-C) are necessary (Harris et al., 2016) and that Polycomb group (PcG) proteins are necessary for the silencing activity of BRV-C.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: A binding site of the PcG DNA binding factor Pleiohomeotic (Pho) is present in BRV-C.
source: Indeed, a binding site of the PcG DNA binding factor Pleiohomeotic (Pho) (Mohd-Sarip et al., 2002) is present in BRV-C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A 17 bp sequence from region 6/7 of BRV-C is present within an enhancer previously identified in the Mmp1 locus.
source: By conducting BLAST searches of the genome using sequences from these highly conserved regions, we found an exact copy of a 17 bp sequence from region 6/7 present within an enhancer previously identified in the Matrix metalloproteinase 1 (Mmp1) locus (Figure 1B, Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, with citation to previous work identifying the Mmp1 enhancer.

claim: Part of the 17 bp sequence matches an Sp1 binding site.
source: We compared this 17 bp sequence with a library of known Drosophila transcription factor binding sites using a motif comparison tool (Gupta et al., 2007) and found that part of this sequence matches an Sp1 binding site (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, with citation to the motif comparison tool.

claim: Sp1 binding sites are required for the activity of Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) and have been identified in most molecularly-characterized PREs.
source: Sp1 binding sites are known to be required for the activity of Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) and have been identified in most molecularly-characterized PREs (Brown et al., 2005), while an Sp1 family member, Ssps, has been shown to bind different PREs and contribute to silencing (Brown et al., 2005; Brown and Kassis, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Mmp1-GFP reporter is strongly activated upon genetic ablation in early L3 discs in a pattern that resembles endogenous damage-induced Mmp1 protein.
source: In contrast, upon genetic ablation in early L3 discs (day 7) using rn-GAL4, GAL80ts, UAS-eiger (hereafter rnts>egr), the reporter is strongly activated in a pattern that resembles endogenous damage-induced Mmp1 protein (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: JNK signaling is a necessary input into the Mmp1 enhancer for damage-induced expression.
source: Ablation in the absence of JNK activity using a hep mutant background (hep/Y) fails to induce the reporter or Mmp1 (Figure 1H). Thus, JNK signaling is a necessary input into the enhancer, as it is for damage-induced Mmp1 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1H showing lack of reporter activity in hep mutant background.

claim: Ectopic activation of JNK signaling through expression of hepCA leads to strong reporter activation.
source: Conversely, ectopic activation of JNK signaling through expression of hepCA leads to strong reporter activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Physical wounding of discs followed by ex vivo culture results in activation of the Mmp1 reporter at the wound edge, coincident with Mmp1 expression.
source: Physical wounding of these discs followed by ex vivo culture also results in activation of the Mmp1 reporter at the wound edge, coincident with Mmp1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Mmp1-GFP reporter recapitulates the weaker expression of Mmp1 in response to genetic ablation in late L3 discs.
source: Consistently, the Mmp1-GFP reporter also recapitulates the weaker expression of Mmp1 in response to genetic ablation with either egr or rpr in late L3 discs (day 9, Figure 1F–G), despite a robust level of JNK activity, as indicated by the AP-1 reporter (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1F-G.

claim: Mmp1-A can be activated equally as strongly in both early and late L3 discs in the absence of the Mmp1-B sequences.
source: Mmp1-A was strongly activated specifically in response to damage, more so than the full-length enhancer (Figure 1I–J). Moreover, in the absence of the Mmp1-B sequences it can be activated equally as strongly in both early and late L3 discs (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1I-J.

claim: Mmp1-B yields no enhancer activity in ablated young or old discs.
source: In contrast, Mmp1-B, which contains the 17 bp motif and conserved Pho binding site yielded no enhancer activity in ablated young or old discs (Figure 1K–L), despite containing two predicted AP-1 binding sites (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1K-L.

claim: Expression of Mmp1-GFP and Mmp1 protein in a pc15/+ ablated late L3 disc was significantly stronger compared to the wild type control.
source: Expression of Mmp1-GFP and Mmp1 protein in a pc15/+ ablated late L3 disc was significantly stronger compared to the wild type control (Figure 1M–N), indicating that Polycomb-mediated epigenetic silencing is necessary to limit Mmp1-GFP activation in mature tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1M-N.

claim: Polycomb-mediated epigenetic silencing is necessary to limit Mmp1-GFP activation in mature tissues.
source: Expression of Mmp1-GFP and Mmp1 protein in a pc15/+ ablated late L3 disc was significantly stronger compared to the wild type control (Figure 1M–N), indicating that Polycomb-mediated epigenetic silencing is necessary to limit Mmp1-GFP activation in mature tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data shown in Figures 1M-N.

claim: The age-dependent silencing of the Mmp1 enhancer is dependent upon PcG function.
source: Also, like DRMSWnt, its age-dependent silencing is dependent upon PcG function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data showing increased expression in pc mutant background.

claim: Only a small number of peaks in each pairwise comparison of ATAC-seq data met with a standard statistical cutoff (padj <0.05).
source: When analyzing the chromatin accessibility data, we were surprised to find that only a small number of peaks in each pairwise comparison met with a standard statistical cutoff (padj <0.05), particularly when comparing chromatin profiles of damaged and undamaged discs (151 altered in early L3 with 90 becoming more accessible, 27 altered in late L3 with 16 becoming more accessible, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: The small number of statistically significant peaks is likely due to the use of whole discs in the ATAC-seq protocol, as signals from regenerating cells only comprise a small portion of the disc.
source: We speculate that this is likely due to the use of whole discs in our protocol, as signals from regenerating cells only comprise a small portion of the disc and are potentially diluted by the chromatin profile of cells of undamaged tissue.
evidence: This is stated as speculation to explain the observation.

claim: 222 regions become more open upon damage in early L3 compared to undamaged controls, and 33 become more accessible in late L3 discs (using padj <0.1 and log2FC >0.5).
source: Using these cutoffs, we observe the same trend but now identify 222 regions that become more open upon damage in early L3 compared to undamaged controls, and 33 that become more accessible in late L3 discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: 12 regions consistently open upon damage at both early and late L3 time points.
source: Of these, 12 regions consistently open upon damage at both time points.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: The chromatin landscape is more responsive to damage in immature than mature discs.
source: Thus, the chromatin landscape, at least as assessed by this criterion, is more responsive to damage in immature than mature discs, which in principle could contribute to the reduction in regenerative capacity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the ATAC-seq data showing more damage-responsive regions in early L3 than late L3.

claim: 729 regions are significantly less accessible in damaged late L3 discs versus damaged early L3, and therefore become silenced with maturity in the context of damage.
source: When comparing damaged discs at the different developmental timepoints, there are 729 regions that are significantly less accessible in damaged late L3 discs versus damaged early L3, and therefore become silenced with maturity in the context of damage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: 28 (13.3%) of the 222 early L3 damage-responsive regions are included in the maturity-silenced category, identifying them as putative DRMS regions.
source: We find that 28 (13.3%) of the 222 early L3 damage-responsive are included in this category, thus identifying them as putative damage-responsive and maturity-silenced (DRMS) regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 28 DRMS peaks are enriched at genomic locations categorized as actively transcribed introns and other open chromatin, while being relatively reduced at actively transcribed promoters and exons.
source: Assaying the position of the 28 DRMS peaks relative to the total open chromatin detected by ATAC-seq shows they are enriched at genomic locations categorized as actively transcribed introns and other open chromatin, while being relatively reduced at actively transcribed promoters and exons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; Kharchenko et al., 2011), consistent with these peaks localizing to enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, with citation to chromatin state definitions.

claim: Both the wg/Wnt6 and Mmp1 enhancer regions become more accessible upon damage in early L3 discs, but not in late L3.
source: Visualizing the chromatin accessibility at the experimentally validated wg/Wnt6 and Mmp1 enhancer loci shows that both regions become more accessible upon damage in early L3 discs, but not in late L3, consistent with DRMS behavior (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: The Mmp1-US enhancer shows damage-responsive and maturity-silenced behavior.
source: We generated a GFP reporter to the region spanning this region (Mmp1-US-GFP) and observed damage-responsive, maturity-silenced expression correlating with its accessibility indicated by ATAC-seq (Figure 2C–C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2C-C'.

claim: Regenerative Mmp1 expression is likely regulated via multiple enhancers.
source: These results show that regenerative Mmp1 expression is likely regulated via multiple enhancers, and that our approach can be successful in identifying actual enhancers that are both damage-responsive and maturity-silenced.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the identification of multiple DRMS enhancers near Mmp1.

claim: Several genes known to be involved in regeneration are adjacent to damage-responsive peaks, including kay, upd1 and zfh2.
source: Several genes known to be involved in the regeneration are adjacent to damage-responsive peaks, including kay, upd1 and zfh2 (La Fortezza et al., 2016; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work and reference to supplementary data.

claim: Four candidate DRMS regions near CG9572, ftz-f1, apt and bru2 function as damage-responsive enhancers that are silenced with maturity.
source: All four reporters were tested under both ablated and unablated conditions in early and late L3 discs, and each showed damage-induced expression in early L3 discs of varying strength (Figure 2E–H). Importantly this expression was consistently reduced in late L3 ablated discs (Figure 2E'–H'), and none of the regions tested showed activity during development in undamaged L3 discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D). Thus, the DNA corresponding to these peaks are bona fide damage-responsive enhancers that are silenced with maturity, similar to the DRMSWnt and DRMSMmp1 enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E-H, 2E'-H', and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: DUAL Control uses the bacterial transcriptional regulator LexA and its binding motif LexAOp as an independent alternative to GAL4/UAS.
source: This system uses the bacterial transcriptional regulator LexA and its binding motif LexAOp, which have been used in Drosophila as an independent alternative to GAL4/UAS (Lai and Lee, 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: DUAL Control permits tissue-specific ablation of the medial wing pouch in response to a heat shock, independent of GAL4/UAS.
source: We combined these two transgenes with either lexAOp-rpr or lexAOp-egr, resulting in a system that permits tissue-specific ablation of the medial wing pouch in response to a heat shock, and which is entirely independent of GAL4/UAS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: A single heat shock can simultaneously induce a pulse of LexA-driven ablation of the medial pouch and activate sustained GAL4 expression in the surrounding cells that contribute to the regenerated pouch.
source: Thus, a single heat shock can simultaneously induce a pulse of LexA-driven ablation of the medial pouch and activate sustained GAL4 expression in the surrounding cells that contribute to the regenerated pouch (Figure 3C–D; Herrera et al., 2013; Verghese and Su, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3C-D, with citations to previous work.

claim: Both the LexA and the GAL4 components of DUAL Control can be activated with a single 37°C heat shock of duration as short as 10 min, but a single 45 min heat shock was optimal.
source: We found that both the LexA and the GAL4 components of the system can be activated with a single 37°C heat shock of duration as short as 10 min, but that a single 45 min heat shock was optimal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Cells expressing rpr can be detected within 6 hr post-heat shock (PHS) using DUAL Control.
source: We then examined a time course of ablation using rpr with DUAL Control DVE>>GAL4 (Figure 3G–K) and found that cells expressing rpr (dGFP positive) can be detected within 6 hr post-heat shock (PHS, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: At 6 hr PHS the majority of the salm domain stains positively for activated caspase, which is mostly observed within the disc proper.
source: At this time point the majority of the salm domain stains positively for activated caspase, which is mostly observed within the disc proper (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At 18 hr PHS the majority of cell corpses had been extruded basally from the disc.
source: At 18 hr PHS the majority of cell corpses had been extruded basally from the disc (Figure 3F and J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3F and J.

claim: At 24 hr PHS the epithelium had mostly regained a normal appearance and by 48 hr PHS the associated debris was minimal, while regeneration was complete.
source: At 24 hr the epithelium had mostly regained a normal appearance and by 48 hr PHS the associated debris was minimal, while regeneration was complete (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3K.

claim: UAS-RFP expression resulting from heat shock induced DVE>>GAL4 was observed at 6 hr PHS in the cells surrounding the ablated salm domain, and persisted throughout the recovery period.
source: By comparison, UAS-RFP expression resulting from heat shock induced DVE>>GAL4 was observed at 6 hr PHS (Figure 3H) in the cells surrounding the ablated salm domain, and persisted throughout the recovery period (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that cells that drive the regenerative growth can be targeted for manipulation using DUAL Control, and that ablation and UAS-driven gene expression can be temporally and spatially separated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3H-K.

claim: When ablated in early L3 using DUAL Control with rpr, around 95% of wings produced were in the 'wild type' or 'nicked' category, indicating that regeneration was mostly complete.
source: When ablated in early L3, around 95% of wings produced were in the 'wild type' or 'nicked' category, indicating that regeneration was mostly complete (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Ablation in late L3 using DUAL Control with rpr yielded many more 'full notch' or 'ablated' wings, demonstrating the loss of regenerative capacity in wing discs during development.
source: By comparison, ablation in late L3 yielded many more 'full notch' or 'ablated' wings (Figure 3M), demonstrating the loss of regenerative capacity in wing discs during development.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Ablation with egr using DUAL Control resulted in weaker adult phenotypes and lower levels of activated caspase compared to rpr.
source: Ablation with egr resulted in weaker adult phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and lower levels of activated caspase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Both Wg and Mmp1 protein are detected following ablation with rpr, and more so with egr due to its stronger activation of the JNK pathway.
source: Both Wg and Mmp1 protein are detected following ablation with rpr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), and more so with egr due to its stronger activation of the JNK pathway (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Both DRMS enhancers for wg and Mmp1 are activated by DUAL Control ablation.
source: Both genes have experimentally validated DRMS enhancers, which are activated by DUAL Control ablation (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4A-B.

claim: Targeting either wg or Mmp1 for knockdown with RNAi using DUAL Control strongly decreases the damage-induced expression of both proteins.
source: Targeting either wg or Mmp1 for knockdown with RNAi using this system strongly decreases the damage-induced expression of both proteins, while the amount of cell death appears unaffected (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4C-D.

claim: The extent of regeneration is reduced when wg or Mmp1 are knocked down using DUAL Control.
source: The extent of regeneration, as assessed by the change in adult wing phenotypes in response to ablation with rpr, is reduced in each case (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Knockdown of Mmp1 for the same duration in the absence of ablation yields little to no effect on adult wings.
source: Knockdown of Mmp1 for the same duration in the absence of ablation yields little to no effect on adult wings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), while knockdown of wg without ablation produces patterning defects localized to the distal wing edge (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) that are clearly distinguishable from the wing tissue loss that follows ablation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: wg is required for both regrowth following damage and repatterning.
source: Thus, wg is required for both regrowth following damage and repatterning.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of Myc using RNAi directed to regenerating tissue with DUAL Control following ablation with rpr showed a dramatic reduction in regeneration.
source: Knockdown of Myc using RNAi directed to regenerating tissue with either DUAL Control PDM>>GAL4 or DVE>>GAL4 following ablation with rpr showed a dramatic reduction in regeneration (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Overexpression of Myc improves adult wing size and morphology following ablation.
source: Consistently, overexpression of Myc improves adult wing size and morphology (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The phenotypes resulting from Myc manipulation likely result from changes in damage-induced proliferation.
source: An E2F reporter (PCNA-GFP) shows that these phenotypes likely result from changes in damage-induced proliferation in response to altered levels of Myc (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4G-J.

claim: Knockdown of upd1 or upd2 appears to strongly reduce regeneration.
source: Knockdown of the JAK/STAT upd1 or upd2 appears to strongly reduce regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), while knockdown of upd3, which does not have a damage-responsive peak, also mildly reduces regeneration but the effect is less significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knockdown of the transcription factor Stat92E or receptor domeless (dome) results in less-complete wings, confirming the requirement for JAK/STAT signaling in regenerating tissue.
source: Knockdown of the transcription factor Stat92E or receptor domeless (dome) also results in less-complete wings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), confirming the requirement for JAK/STAT signaling in regenerating tissue surrounding the ablation domain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CG9572 is predicted to encode a 441 amino acid protein of unknown function.
source: CG9572 is predicted to encode a 441 amino acid protein of unknown function.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the gene.

claim: CG9572 has strong sequence similarity to the EGF domain repeats of the Jagged protein.
source: In order to better characterize CG9572, we performed protein blast (blastp) and alignment scoring, which revealed strong sequence similarity to the EGF domain repeats of the Jagged protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a membrane-bound ligand for Notch in vertebrates (Lindsell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Jagged.

claim: The CG9572 peptide sequence is predicted to contain seven EGF-type repeats that each displays a characteristic spacing of cysteine residues.
source: The peptide sequence is predicted to contain seven EGF-type repeats that each displays a characteristic spacing of cysteine residues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: CG9572 has a 14-amino acid hydrophobic stretch close to its N-terminus that is likely to function as a signal peptide.
source: Similar to Jagged, CG9572 also has a 14-amino acid hydrophobic stretch close to its N-terminus that is likely to function as a signal peptide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Unlike Jagged or other Notch ligands, CG9572 lacks a second hydrophobic stretch that would serve as a transmembrane domain, or a Delta/Serrate/LAG-2 (DSL) domain.
source: However, unlike Jagged or other Notch ligands it lacks a second hydrophobic stretch that would serve as a transmembrane domain, or a Delta/Serrate/LAG-2 (DSL) domain characteristic of Notch ligands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When UAS-aspr::HA was expressed in the posterior compartment using en-GAL4, HA staining appeared to be cytoplasmic.
source: When a tagged version, UAS-aspr::HA, was expressed in the posterior compartment using en-GAL4, HA staining appeared to be cytoplasmic (Figure 5B), localizing towards the apical surface of the disc proper (Figure 5C) and with punctae observed in the anterior compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5B-C.

claim: When hh-GAL4 driver was used to express aspr::HA, punctae were observed throughout the anterior compartment consistent with the Aspr protein being secreted from cells.
source: When the stronger hh-GAL4 driver was used, punctae were observed throughout the anterior compartment consistent with the Aspr protein being secreted from cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of aspr in the whole wing pouch using rn-GAL4 does not result in an observable phenotype in the adult wing.
source: Overexpression of aspr in the whole wing pouch using rn-GAL4 does not result in an observable phenotype in the adult wing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), but expression in the posterior compartment infrequently causes abnormal folding in the pouch at the boundary with wild type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: aspr is expressed at low levels in the ventral and lateral areas of undamaged L3 wing discs.
source: In undamaged L3 wing discs, in situ hybridization shows aspr is expressed at low levels in the ventral and lateral areas of the disc at low levels (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5E-F.

claim: Upon damage in early L3 discs, aspr is upregulated strongly in the region of the blastema.
source: Upon damage in early L3 discs, aspr is upregulated strongly in the region of the blastema, as shown in discs ablated by both rnts>egr (Figure 5G,M) and DUAL Control ablation with egr (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5G, I, M.

claim: In damaged discs from late L3 larvae, aspr has much weaker damage-induced expression.
source: In damaged discs from late L3 larvae, aspr has much weaker damage-induced expression (Figure 5H,J,N).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5H, J, N.

claim: Knockdown of aspr in the developing wing pouch using rn-GAL4 in undamaged discs has little effect on adult wing size or patterning.
source: Knockdown of aspr with two different RNAi lines in the developing wing pouch using rn-GAL4 in undamaged discs has little effect on adult wing size or patterning (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Knockdown of aspr in mid L3 discs using en-GAL4 delays the onset of expression of the Notch target cut at the prospective wing margin in the posterior compartment.
source: However, we found that knockdown of aspr in mid L3 discs using en-GAL4 delays the onset of expression of the Notch target cut at the prospective wing margin in the posterior compartment (Figure 5O–Q), suggesting aspr might promote Notch signaling during normal development.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5O-Q.

claim: Knockdown of aspr results in weak reduction in fluorescence of a Notch reporter, NRE-GFP.
source: This is also shown by the weak reduction in fluorescence of a Notch reporter, NRE-GFP (Zacharioudaki and Bray, 2014; Figure 5R–S).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5R-S, with citation to the reporter.

claim: Aspr is a secreted regulator of Notch signaling in the wing, which is strongly activated in regenerating tissue upon damage.
source: These data suggest that Aspr is a secreted regulator of Notch signaling in the wing, which is strongly activated in regenerating tissue upon damage.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data.

claim: Knockdown of aspr using DUAL Control reduces the extent of regeneration.
source: To address whether aspr is necessary for regeneration, we used DUAL Control to reduce its expression in regenerating cells in mid-L3 discs using the two different RNAi lines following rpr ablation of the wing pouch. At this stage Cut expression at the margin is beginning to be established (Figure 5R), while ablation at an earlier stage leads to a delay in development and hinders Cut expression. Upon aspr knockdown the presence of Cut in these discs is markedly reduced (Figure 5T–U), suggesting that ablation combined with the loss of aspr may limit Cut expression that has already been initiated. The extent of regeneration is also decreased (Figure 5V).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5T-U, V.

claim: aspr hemizygous animals (Mi[MIC]CG9572[MI02471]/Y) show a strongly decreased ability to regenerate when ablated with DUAL Control.
source: aspr hemizygous animals have no obvious developmental defects but show a strongly decreased ability to regenerate when ablated with DUAL Control (Figure 5V) and rnts>egr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5V and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Expression of Aspr::HA does not strongly affect regeneration.
source: Expression of Aspr::HA does not strongly affect regeneration (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H), indicating that while it is necessary for regeneration, ectopic expression alone it is not sufficient to improve it, as we have demonstrated with other pro-regeneration genes such as wg (Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H, with citation to previous work.

claim: The strongest damage-responsive change in chromatin accessibility of all detected DRMS peaks was at the apontic (apt) gene.
source: From our ATAC-seq dataset we noted that the strongest damage-responsive change in chromatin accessibility of all detected DRMS peaks was at the apontic (apt) gene (Figure 2D, Figure 6A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 6A.

claim: DNA spanning peak 4931 at the apt locus functions as a DRMS enhancer in vivo.
source: We have shown that DNA spanning this peak (Peak 4931) does indeed function as a DRMS enhancer in vivo (Figure 2G–G'), while the data of Khan et al. shows that apt is transcriptionally upregulated in blastema cells (Khan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2G-G', with citation to Khan et al.

claim: apt encodes a b-Zip transcription factor that has been characterized in tracheal development and formation of both male and female germlines.
source: apt is also known as trachea defective (tdf), and encodes a b-Zip transcription factor that has been characterized in tracheal development (Eulenberg and Schuh, 1997; Gellon et al., 1997) and formation of both male and female germlines (Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Monahan and Starz-Gaiano, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claim: In the male germline, decreasing apt function results in increased expression of JAK/STAT targets, suggesting apt functions to restrict JAK/STAT signaling.
source: In the male germline, decreasing apt function results in increased expression of JAK/STAT targets, suggesting apt functions, at least in this context, to restrict JAK/STAT signaling (Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Monahan and Starz-Gaiano, 2016), which is known to be required for wing disc regeneration (Katsuyama et al., 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claim: Apt is expressed at high levels in the squamous cells of the peripodial epithelium and tracheal tubes of undamaged developing wing discs throughout L3.
source: Using an antibody that recognizes the Apt protein (Liu et al., 2003), we found that Apt is expressed at high levels in the squamous cells of the peripodial epithelium and tracheal tubes of undamaged developing wing discs throughout L3, and expression is not obviously above background in cells of the disc proper (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B, with citation to the antibody.

claim: Apt can be detected in the disc proper following damage in early L3, but not in late L3.
source: However, optical section imaging of ablated discs shows that Apt can be detected in the disc proper following damage in early L3 (Figure 6B), but not in late L3 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Knockdown of apt in regeneration-competent early L3 discs using DUAL Control results in adult wings that are more complete than in ablated controls.
source: To test whether apt is necessary for regeneration, we reduced its expression using DUAL Control by expressing an apt RNAi transgene in regeneration-competent early L3 discs. In view of the demonstration that apt can promote wing growth by promoting Hedgehog expression (Wang et al., 2017), we were surprised to find that the adult wings were more complete than in ablated controls not expressing the apt RNAi (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D, with citation to previous work.

claim: Knockdown of apt in late L3 discs using DUAL Control results in adult wings that are more complete than in controls.
source: We then examined the effect of apt knockdown in late L3 discs and found that, once again, adult wings were more complete than in controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: apt normally acts to limit regeneration following damage.
source: These observations indicate that apt knockdown either protects discs from damage during the ablation phase or promotes regeneration. Since the levels of cleaved caspase DCP1 appeared similar in the presence and absence of apt knockdown (Figure 6E–F), this suggests that apt normally acts to limit regeneration following damage.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: A hypomorphic apt mutant (aptK15608/+) shows a mild increase in regenerative ability compared to wild type at both time points when ablated with DUAL Control and rnts>egr.
source: This is corroborated by a hypomorphic apt mutant (aptK15608/+, [Eulenberg and Schuh, 1997]), which also shows a mild increase in regenerative ability compared to wild type at both time points when ablated with DUAL Control and rnts>egr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D, with citation to the mutant.

claim: With apt knockdown, there is an increase in the activity of a Stat92E reporter specifically in blastema cells.
source: We observed the expression of a fluorescent Stat92E reporter (STAT-GFP) in late L3 discs ablated with DUAL Control in the presence of apt knockdown. Normally at this stage, STAT activity is minimal in regenerating cells of ablated discs (Figure 6E). However, with apt knockdown, we found an increase in the activity of this reporter specifically in blastema cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6E-F.

claim: apt might affect regeneration by influencing JAK/STAT activity.
source: As apt is known to act in the germline to limit JAK/STAT signaling, we examined whether it might affect regeneration by influencing JAK/STAT activity.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on known function of apt.

claim: Inhibition of extra sex combs (esc) specifically during the regeneration period consistently improved regeneration, even in discs ablated in early L3.
source: However, inhibition of the Polycomb group gene extra sex combs (esc), which encodes a component of the PRC2 complex (reviewed by Kassis et al., 2017), specifically during the regeneration period consistently improved regeneration, even in discs ablated in early L3 (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I, with citation to review of PRC2 complex.

claim: Even a small reduction in esc levels is likely to improve regeneration.
source: Under these conditions, we observed no adult wing defects when esc was knocked down in unablated wings for this short duration (data not shown). Thus, even a small reduction in esc levels is likely to improve regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the observation that knockdown doesn't cause developmental defects.

claim: Ablation in a heterozygous esc background (esc5/+) leads to improved regeneration when ablated with rnts>egr.
source: Ablation in a heterozygous esc background (esc5/+) similarly leads to improved regeneration when ablated with rnts>egr (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), although this effect was not significant when ablated using DUAL Control, unlike targeted knockdown with RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The level of GFP expression from DRMSWnt, DRMSMmp1, and DRMSaspr reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls.
source: To test whether the improved regenerative capacity of esc knockdown was due to alteration of DRMS activity, we examined the activity of three different DRMS reporters, DRMSWnt, DRMSMmp1, and DRMSaspr, in late L3 discs expressing escRNAi. The level of GFP expression from all of the reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls, as was wg and Mmp1 expression (Figure 6J–K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G), indicating that the loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6J-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-G.

claim: The loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
source: The level of GFP expression from all of the reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls, as was wg and Mmp1 expression (Figure 6J–K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G), indicating that the loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data.

claim: Reducing Polycomb-mediated silencing appears capable of overcoming the suppression of a regeneration program that operates simultaneously at multiple loci in the genome.
source: Thus, reducing Polycomb-mediated silencing appears capable of overcoming the suppression of a regeneration program that operates simultaneously at multiple loci in the genome.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claim: The reduced expression of wg and Wnt6 elicited by damage as discs mature can be explained by the properties of a damage-responsive and maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancer that lies between the two genes.
source: We previously showed that the reduced expression of wg and Wnt6 elicited by damage as discs mature can be explained by the properties of a damage-responsive and maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancer that lies between the two genes (Harris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work with citation.

claim: Manipulating the DRMSWnt enhancer by deleting the maturity silencing module restores damage-responsive wg expression in mature discs, but this alone is insufficient to preserve regenerative capacity.
source: Manipulating this enhancer by deleting the maturity silencing module restores damage-responsive wg expression in mature discs, but this alone is insufficient to preserve regenerative capacity at this stage of development.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: The overall effect of the expression of multiple genes regulated by DRMS enhancers is to promote regeneration.
source: Since the manipulation of a chromatin silencing factor, esc, can de-repress at least three DRMS enhancers, and also promote regeneration, it is likely that the overall effect of the expression of multiple genes regulated by DRMS enhancers is to promote regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claim: The number of DRMS regions identified using ATAC-seq are likely to be an underestimate since the assay examined chromatin changes using whole discs, in which only a small proportion of cells are undergoing regeneration.
source: However, it is important to note that the number of regions we identified using ATAC-seq are likely to be an underestimate since our assay examined chromatin changes using whole discs, in which only a small proportion of cells are undergoing regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the ATAC-seq approach.

claim: Knockdown of aspr adversely impacted regenerative growth but produced no obvious effect on the normal development of the wing except perhaps a delay in the development of the wing margin.
source: Knockdown of aspr adversely impacted regenerative growth but produced no obvious effect on the normal development of the wing except perhaps a delay in the development of the wing margin.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the aspr knockdown experiments.

claim: Following aspr knockdown, expression of the markers at the margin such as Cut and the Notch reporter was delayed both in normal and regenerating discs.
source: We have shown that following aspr knockdown, expression of the markers at the margin such as Cut and the Notch reporter was delayed both in normal and regenerating discs, suggesting that aspr could potentially promote Notch signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the aspr knockdown experiments.

claim: Aspr has sequence similarity to the vertebrate Notch ligand Jagged.
source: Our analysis reveals that Aspr has sequence similarity to the vertebrate Notch ligand Jagged (Lindsell et al., 1995), raising the possibility that its influence on Notch signaling could be as a ligand.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis with citation.

claim: Unlike most Notch ligands characterized to date, Aspr lacks a DSL domain or a predicted transmembrane domain.
source: However, unlike most Notch ligands characterized to date, Aspr lacks a DSL domain or a predicted transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: Non-canonical Notch ligands that lack a DSL domain have been identified in mammals and have been shown to regulate Notch signaling when engineered into Drosophila.
source: Non-canonical Notch ligands that lack a DSL domain have been identified in mammals (Baladrón et al., 2005; Falix et al., 2012) and have been shown to regulate Notch signaling when engineered into Drosophila (Bray et al., 2008), while several Notch ligands have been characterized in C. elegans that lack transmembrane domains (Chen and Greenwald, 2004; Komatsu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: Being anchored to the membrane is thought to be crucial for the mechanism by which Notch ligands function in Drosophila.
source: Being anchored to the membrane is thought to be crucial for the mechanism by which Notch ligands function in Drosophila; endocytosis of the ligand engaged to Notch is presumed to generate the mechanical force that alters Notch conformation and renders it susceptible to proteolytic cleavage, which eventually results in nuclear translocation of the intracellular domain (Parks et al., 2000; Langridge and Struhl, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: It is unlikely that Aspr could function as a canonical Notch ligand based on the view that membrane anchoring is crucial for Notch activation.
source: Thus, at least based on this view of Notch signaling, it is unlikely that Aspr could function as a canonical Notch ligand.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the lack of transmembrane domain and current understanding of Notch signaling.

claim: Notch signaling is thought to function as part of double repressive mechanism that controls regenerative growth.
source: Moreover, Notch signaling is thought to function as part of double repressive mechanism (Herranz et al., 2008) that controls regenerative growth (Smith-Bolton et al., 2009), and is reduced in blastema cells to permit Myc-dependent growth.
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: Overexpression of aspr did not appear to increase Notch signaling, at least as assessed by activation of the Notch reporter.
source: Importantly, overexpression of aspr did not appear to increase Notch signaling, at least as assessed by activation of the Notch reporter.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The role of Aspr in promoting regeneration could be independent of a direct influence on Notch signaling.
source: Therefore, the role of Aspr in promoting regeneration could be independent of a direct influence on Notch signaling and remains to be explored further.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claim: Knockdown of apt appears to improve regeneration in discs ablated in either early or late L3.
source: In addition to aspr, we also found that the transcriptional regulator apt functions in regeneration, although in contrast to aspr, knockdown of apt appears to improve regeneration in discs ablated in either early or late L3.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the apt knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of apt increased expression of a STAT reporter, suggesting this improvement might be via increased JAK/STAT signaling.
source: Knockdown of apt increased expression of a STAT reporter, suggesting this improvement might be via increased JAK/STAT signaling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data.

claim: Reducing JAK/STAT signaling reduced tissue loss following egr-induced ablation, but did not seem to compromise the extent of compensatory proliferation.
source: A previous study has shown that reducing JAK/STAT signaling reduced tissue loss following egr-induced ablation, but did not seem to compromise the extent of compensatory proliferation (La Fortezza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claim: Overexpression of upd1 or upd2 concurrently with ablation did not improve regeneration.
source: Furthermore, the overexpression of upd1 or upd2 concurrently with ablation did not improve regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Reducing esc activity derepressed at least three DRMS enhancers that were tested using reporter gene constructs.
source: We also found that reducing PcG-mediated repression via knockdown of esc improved overall regeneration. Reducing esc activity derepressed at least three DRMS enhancers that were tested using reporter gene constructs.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the esc knockdown experiments.

claim: It is likely that many DRMS enhancers are regulated by Polycomb-mediated silencing.
source: Since a reduction in esc levels alleviates silencing at multiple DRMS enhancers, it is likely that many of these other enhancers are also regulated by Polycomb-mediated silencing, as for DRMSWnt.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claim: Enhancer accessibility is an important mechanism that regulates various properties of imaginal discs, including specification of their identity during development and cellular proliferation.
source: These findings parallel those of other groups who have used chromatin profiling in imaginal discs to show that enhancer accessibility is an important mechanism that regulates various properties of imaginal discs, including specification of their identity during development and cellular proliferation (McKay and Lieb, 2013; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: Distal enhancers for key cell cycle regulators such as cyclin E and string become less accessible as development proceeds, independently of cell-cycle status.
source: In a recent study that investigated the basis of terminal exit from the cell cycle in cells of the Drosophila wing disc (Ma et al., 2019) it was found that distal enhancers for key cell cycle regulators such as cyclin E and string become less accessible as development proceeds. This occurs independently of cell-cycle status but instead seems to be governed by a temporal program.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claim: The robust exit from the cell-cycle could potentially be explained by reduced levels of many cell-cycle regulators caused by the silencing of enhancers at multiple loci.
source: The robust exit from the cell-cycle could potentially be explained by reduced levels of many cell-cycle regulators caused by the silencing of enhancers at multiple loci.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings from Ma et al., 2019.

claim: An enhancer-mediated mechanism that reduces the expression of multiple genes necessary for regeneration in mature discs might be more robust than one that relies on reduced expression of a single key regulator.
source: Similarly, an enhancer-mediated mechanism that reduces the expression of multiple genes necessary for regeneration in mature discs might be more robust than one that relies on reduced expression of a single key regulator.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: If regeneration in maturing discs is suppressed by the silencing of multiple DRMS enhancers, it could be restored by alleviating the silencing at multiple DRMS enhancers or by activating pathways that function downstream of genes that promote regeneration.
source: If regeneration in maturing discs is indeed suppressed by the silencing of multiple DRMS enhancers that regulate genes promoting regeneration, it could be restored, at least in principle, in two different ways. One would be by alleviating the silencing at multiple DRMS enhancers; knockdown of esc likely functions in this way. Another way would be by activating pathways that function downstream of genes that promote regeneration (bypass suppression).
evidence: This is stated as speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway can promote plasticity during regeneration.
source: Our previous work (Worley et al., 2018) has shown that the JAK/STAT pathway can promote plasticity during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Damage-responsive enhancers have been identified in multiple species and found to share common regulators, including JNK signaling.
source: Damage-responsive enhancers have been identified in multiple species and found to share common regulators, including JNK signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The lepb gene in zebrafish appears to be regulated by a damage-responsive enhancer, which is altered epigenetically following injury to fins or the heart, and requires AP-1 binding sites for activation of gene expression.
source: The lepb gene in zebrafish appears to be regulated by such an enhancer, which is altered epigenetically following injury to fins or the heart, and requires AP-1 binding sites for activation of gene expression (Kang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claim: Discrete regulatory elements that regulate muscle regeneration, bone fracture and soft-tissue injury have been described in mice.
source: In mice, discrete regulatory elements that regulate muscle regeneration, bone fracture and soft-tissue injury have also been described (Guenther et al., 2015; Aguilar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: It is not known whether damage-responsive enhancers in zebrafish become less active with maturity since zebrafish preserve their regenerative capacity and adult mice continue to heal muscle and fractured bones.
source: However, it is not known whether these enhancers become less active with maturity since zebrafish preserve their regenerative capacity and adult mice continue to heal muscle and fractured bones.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: The murine neonatal heart loses regenerative ability within the first week of life.
source: In contrast, the murine neonatal heart is known to lose regenerative ability within the first week of life (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claim: There is evidence that damage-responsive regulatory elements are conserved in the human genome and function in models of human epithelial injury.
source: Finally, there is evidence that damage-responsive regulatory elements are conserved in the human genome (Suzuki et al., 2019) and function in models of human epithelial injury (Lander et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: The study of damage-responsive enhancers and the mechanism by which they regulate the response to injury could provide important insights in human regenerative medicine in future.
source: Thus, the study of these enhancers and the mechanism by which they regulate the response to injury could provide important insights in human regenerative medicine in future.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about future implications.
